after:
The refusal names WHICH fields differ and never what they now hold, since a refusal is written to a log that a human who approved none of the new text will read, and quoting it there would publish unapproved content through the refusal path. (Amended APRV-224, pending sign-off.)

That comparison MUST run before the token is consumed. A drifted draft refuses with nothing appended, no `execution.started`, and the grant intact, so the same token sends once the approved text is restored and a third attempt is then refused as a spent one. Running it after the spend was a defect (APRV-276), found on a live inbox: the refusal was correct and it burned the human's single-use authority anyway, and a refusal that costs a person another tap teaches that person to stop checking, which is the one lesson this whole design cannot afford to teach. The rule generalises past this adapter, and it is the same rule the declared-credential resolution above states: a condition that makes the side effect impossible, and that the runtime can establish without attempting it, MUST be established before the token is spent. The reference runtime gives adapters one place to put such a condition, an optional pre-token check the contract calls between the credential resolution and the token spend, whose refusals carry the adapter's own reason and append nothing. A pre-token check never replaces the same check inside the send window: the implementation compares the draft a second time immediately before the send, because a draft is remote mutable state and something has to bound the gap between the last read and the send. A drift caught by the second comparison is an `execution.started` followed by an `execution.failed`, which is the honest record of a window that was open when the far side moved.

Which key performs the pre-spend comparison is decided here rather than left to a deployment, because it decides who chooses the bytes the check reads. It is the SENDING key from the vault, read through the same pre-token credential window this section already opens for an adapter's declared credentials, and it is never a key the calling agent supplies from its own environment. The agent's composing key would work on the wire and would put the party under oversight in charge of the input to its own scrutiny, which §11.1's fourth invariant forbids. Nothing about the vault rule is weakened to allow this: what that rule governs is the window a credential may be read in, and this is the window an implementation already reads credentials in before the spend, entered only when the caller holds the token the human's grant minted. (Amended APRV-276, pending sign-off.)
